# Titles, Captions, and Tables

## Every figure needs a title

- A visualization conveys information and makes a point, so give it context
- The title says what the figure is about and what point it makes
- In a printed document the title is the first part of the caption, below the figure
- A figure can have only one title
- Web or slide figures can carry the title inside the image instead

## The title is not a description

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
- Good: "Corruption and human development: the most developed countries have the least corruption"
- Not: "This figure shows how corruption is related to human development"
- A title can be a short sentence making a clear assertion
- Then add data source and other details

:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
:::
::::

```{r}
#| output: asis
place_fig("fig-corruption-development", fig_corruption_development(),
          w = 7, h = 4.9, x = 7.4, y = 2, width = 8.4)
```

## Axis and legend titles

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Axes and legends need titles too
- State the variable *and* its units: body mass (g), head length (mm), skull size (mm)
- Legend titles explain what color and size encode

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
:::
::::

```{r}
#| output: asis
place_fig("fig-blue-jays-bubbles", fig_blue_jays_bubbles(),
          w = 5.5, h = 4.2, x = 8, y = 2, width = 7.5)
```

## When a title can be omitted

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- A legend with "female" and "male" is self-explanatory
- Country names and movie titles need no "country" or "movie" title
- Years on an x axis need no title here: context is clear

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
:::
::::

```{r}
#| output: asis
place_fig("fig-tech-stocks-minimal-labeling", fig_tech_stocks_minimal_labeling(),
          w = 5, h = 3.4, x = 8, y = 2, width = 7.5)
```

## But do not push it too far

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Without a y axis title, the reader cannot tell what the values are
- Do not assume the plot title or subtitle defines the axes

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
:::
::::

```{r}
#| output: asis
place_fig("fig-tech-stocks-no-axis-titles", fig_tech_stocks_no_axis_titles(),
          w = 5, h = 3.4, x = 8, y = 2, width = 7.5)
```

## And do not overdo it either

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- "company" on a legend of well-known companies adds nothing
- "time (years AD)" is awkward for a few recent years
- Excessive labeling is clutter

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
:::
::::

```{r}
#| output: asis
place_fig("fig-tech-stocks-overlabeled", fig_tech_stocks_overlabeled(),
          w = 5, h = 3.4, x = 8, y = 2, width = 7.5)
```

## Omitting the axis altogether

- Pie charts, treemaps, and mosaic plots often have no explicit axes
- Bar charts can drop an axis if meaning is otherwise clear
- Dropping tick labels signals that qualitative features matter more than exact values

## Tables: layout rules

- No vertical lines
- No horizontal lines between data rows (a line under the header or around the table is fine)
- Left-align text columns
- Right-align number columns, with the same number of decimals throughout
- Center single-character columns
- Align headers with their data
- To guide the eye, use alternating light shading, not lines

## Captions: figures below, tables above

- Readers look at a figure first and read the caption for context, so the caption goes below
- Tables are read like text, top to bottom, so the caption goes above
